metadata.title: DevSecOps Failure Modes & Postmortem-Style Knowledge
metadata.description: Real-world failure scenarios distilled from public postmortems and common cloud incidents. Each entry pairs the failure with its root cause, the controls that would have prevented it, and the detection signals that would have caught it earlier.
source_alignment: Public AWS customer postmortems (Capital One 2019 SSRF, Code Spaces 2014, Tesla Kubernetes 2018)

entries.concept: Public S3 bucket leaks customer data
entries.description: A developer creates an S3 bucket for a one-off export, sets ACL to public-read 'just to share with the partner', forgets to revert it. A bucket-enumeration scanner finds it weeks later. The file contains PII or credentials. This is the most common cloud data-leak pattern in public DBIR data and continues to dominate cloud breaches in 2024-2025.
preventive_controls: Enable S3 Block Public Access at the ACCOUNT level — overrides any bucket-level setting
Enable S3 Block Public Access at the ORGANIZATION level via SCP — even break-glass admins cannot toggle off
Default encryption with KMS CMK — even on accidental public exposure, the object is encrypted
Use IAM Access Analyzer for S3 — flags any bucket reachable from outside the org
Use bucket policies that explicitly deny `s3:GetObject` when `aws:PrincipalOrgID` does not match
detection_signals: Access Analyzer finding 'External access granted to bucket'
GuardDuty finding `Discovery:S3/MaliciousIPCaller.Custom`
CloudTrail `PutBucketAcl` or `PutBucketPolicy` events outside the change-management window
Macie sensitive-data discovery on a bucket newly flagged public
remediation_runbook: Immediately make bucket private (set ACL private, attach explicit deny policy)
Enumerate access via S3 server access logs and CloudFront logs (if fronted)
Identify objects accessed and notify per breach-disclosure obligations
Rotate any credentials, tokens, or keys present in the leaked objects
Add the bucket to weekly Access Analyzer review until permanently retired
anti_patterns: Relying on bucket-level Block Public Access only — account-level is the right layer
Treating 'private bucket with a presigned URL' as the same as a public bucket — presigned URLs in logs/Slack are a separate exposure class
Not enabling S3 server access logs — without them, breach scope cannot be determined

entries.concept: Application SSRF reaches IMDS and steals instance role credentials (Capital One 2019 pattern)
entries.description: An application has an SSRF vulnerability (often via image-fetch or webhook validation). Attacker forces the app to GET http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/<role>. IMDSv1 returns role credentials. Attacker uses them to enumerate and exfiltrate S3 data. This is the Capital One 2019 pattern — 100M records, $190M total cost.
preventive_controls: ENFORCE IMDSv2 (HttpTokens=required) on every instance and launch template — IMDSv2 requires a session token that SSRF cannot easily acquire
BLOCK PUT to /latest/api/token in WAF/proxy and SET IMDSv2 hop-limit=1 (default 2) for non-containerized workloads
USE IRSA in EKS (no IMDS exposure to pods) — pods get credentials via projected SA token, not metadata service
MINIMIZE the role attached to compute — SSRF stealing a role with `s3:Get*` on one bucket is incident-class lower than stealing AdministratorAccess
USE VPC endpoint policies and SG egress rules to limit where stolen credentials can be used FROM (less effective but layered)
detection_signals: GuardDuty `UnauthorizedAccess:IAMUser/InstanceCredentialExfiltration.OutsideAWS`
CloudTrail `AssumeRole` or API calls from the instance role with sourceIPAddress outside the expected VPC NAT range
Sudden spike in `s3:ListBuckets` or `s3:GetObject` from an instance role
WAF logs showing requests to internal IPs (169.254.x.x) in URL parameters
remediation_runbook: Revoke active sessions: `aws iam put-role-policy` with a deny-all + condition `aws:TokenIssueTime` < now
Patch the SSRF vulnerability (input validation, internal-IP blocklist, IMDSv2)
Audit CloudTrail for the credential's actions — every API call with the stolen credential
Rotate any data accessed (re-encrypt with new KMS key)
Review and minimize the instance role permissions
anti_patterns: Allowing IMDSv1 for backward compatibility — SSRF defeats it trivially
Granting compute roles broad S3 access ('AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess') — turns SSRF from incident into breach
Application-level SSRF allowlist by hostname only — DNS rebinding bypasses it

entries.concept: Public Kubernetes dashboard or unauthenticated kubelet leads to cluster takeover (Tesla 2018 pattern)
entries.description: An admin exposes the Kubernetes dashboard via a LoadBalancer service for convenience, with anonymous-auth enabled or no authentication. Attacker reaches it, deploys a cryptominer or pivots into the cluster. Tesla's 2018 incident (cryptojacking via exposed Kubernetes dashboard) is the canonical case. Kubelet read-only port (10255) and unauthenticated API server present similar risks.
preventive_controls: NEVER expose the Kubernetes dashboard publicly — port-forward or behind SSO/identity-aware proxy only
DISABLE anonymous auth on the API server (`--anonymous-auth=false`) and on kubelet (`--anonymous-auth=false`)
DISABLE the kubelet read-only port (`--read-only-port=0`)
RESTRICT API server access via SG / authorized networks — public API endpoint should be IP-allowlisted in EKS
ENFORCE PodSecurityStandard `restricted` in every namespace except kube-system
detection_signals: GuardDuty for EKS Runtime Monitoring findings (`CryptoCurrency:Runtime/BitcoinTool.B`)
Unexpected new namespace, Deployment, or DaemonSet in audit logs
Outbound network traffic to known mining pools (Falco rule)
`kubectl auth can-i --as=system:anonymous` returning yes for any verb
remediation_runbook: Rotate cluster admin credentials, all ServiceAccount tokens, and any cloud credentials reachable from the cluster
Audit all workloads for unknown images, init containers, and recently-added DaemonSets
Inspect node-level processes (Falco / runtime detection) for resident malware
Rebuild compromised nodes — assume node OS compromise
anti_patterns: Exposing the dashboard 'temporarily' for a demo — it never gets removed
Treating private subnets as enough — one compromised pod inside the cluster reaches the dashboard too
kubectl proxy in a long-running tmux session — a stolen laptop gives cluster-admin

entries.concept: AWS access key committed to public repo (or even private repo with broad access)
entries.description: Developer commits `.env` or hardcoded key, pushes to GitHub. Within minutes (literally — there are bots scanning new commits), the key is found and used to spin up crypto-mining instances or exfiltrate data. Even private repos are not safe: a contractor with read access, a leaked PAT, or accidental fork can leak the secret.
preventive_controls: PRE-COMMIT hooks: gitleaks or trufflehog blocking commits containing key patterns
GITHUB push protection (free tier as of 2024) — server-side block of detected secrets
ELIMINATE long-lived keys: use OIDC federation from CI to AWS instead of static keys
SCAN repos continuously (gitleaks-action, GitHub secret scanning) — secrets predate push protection
Rotate any committed secret IMMEDIATELY — assume it leaked even if you force-pushed it away. Git history is forever in clones and forks.
detection_signals: GitHub secret-scanning alert
GuardDuty finding for credential use from unexpected geography
AWS CloudTrail showing API calls from a user-agent or source IP not in the expected baseline
Sudden bill spike (mining instances)
remediation_runbook: Deactivate the IAM key immediately, do not just rotate (rotation gives attacker time)
Audit CloudTrail for all actions taken with the key
Look for backdoors: new IAM users, roles, trust policies, lambda functions
Rotate any data or credentials reachable from the key's permissions
Cost-recover: AWS support will often credit fraud-related spend if remediated quickly
anti_patterns: Force-pushing the offending commit and assuming the secret is gone — clones/forks/CI logs still have it
Long-lived IAM access keys for CI when GitHub OIDC federation is available
Storing secrets in CI environment variables instead of a real secret manager (AWS Secrets Manager, Vault)

entries.concept: Malicious npm/pip package included via dependency confusion or typosquat
entries.description: Attacker publishes a package mimicking a legitimate one (typosquat) or exploits dependency confusion (publishing a public package with the same name as an internal one to a public registry; the build system pulls the public one). Build pipeline installs the malicious package; postinstall script exfiltrates env vars including AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY and CI tokens.
preventive_controls: PIN dependencies with lockfiles AND verify integrity (npm `--ignore-scripts` for CI; pip-compile + hash mode)
USE a private registry (Verdaccio, GitHub Packages, AWS CodeArtifact) configured to NEVER fall through to the public registry for internal scopes
NAMESPACE internal packages with a scope (@company/foo) and reserve the scope on npmjs.com
RUN dependency scanners (Snyk, OWASP Dependency-Check, Dependabot) and BLOCK builds on critical findings
DISABLE postinstall scripts in CI (npm ci `--ignore-scripts`) for any build that does not absolutely need them
GENERATE and verify SBOM (CycloneDX or SPDX) on every build for downstream attestation
detection_signals: Sudden new package in lockfile diff — review every dependency add in code review
Build CPU/network spike during install (postinstall scripts doing work)
Egress traffic from CI runner to unknown domains during install
GuardDuty findings on CI runner credentials used from anomalous IPs
remediation_runbook: Remove the malicious package, lock to a known-good version
Rotate every credential the CI build had access to (AWS, registry, signing keys, deploy tokens)
Re-issue any artifacts the compromised build produced
Audit downstream consumers of those artifacts
anti_patterns: Trusting `latest` tag for any dependency — pin versions
Allowing public-registry fallthrough for internal scopes — opens dependency confusion door
Running `npm install` in CI instead of `npm ci` — non-reproducible, ignores lockfile

entries.concept: Bad deploy + missing PodDisruptionBudget + aggressive autoscaler = full outage
entries.description: A new deploy ships a regression. HPA detects elevated error rate as elevated CPU and scales up. New pods are unhealthy. Cluster Autoscaler removes 'idle' nodes to save cost, evicting healthy pods at the same time the rolling deploy progresses. With no PodDisruptionBudget, kube-controller-manager evicts in parallel. All replicas of the service are unavailable simultaneously.
preventive_controls: DEFINE PodDisruptionBudget (`minAvailable: 1` or `maxUnavailable: 25%`) for every Deployment in production
HEALTH PROBES: separate liveness, readiness, and startup probes — readiness gates traffic, liveness restarts, startup tolerates slow boots
PROGRESSIVE delivery: Argo Rollouts or Flagger with metric-based analysis — auto-rollback on error rate / latency regression
DEPLOY across multiple AZs with topology spread constraints — single-AZ failure does not kill the service
PIN HPA min-replicas to ≥2 for any prod service — 'scale to zero' is for dev/staging
detection_signals: PodDisruptionBudget violation events in audit log
Sudden drop in `kube_deployment_status_replicas_available`
Error budget burn-rate alert (multi-window: fast burn 1h + slow burn 6h)
Synthetic check failures coinciding with deploy timestamp
remediation_runbook: Roll back the deploy via Argo Rollouts abort or `kubectl rollout undo`
Pause autoscaler until incident is closed
Add PDB before next deploy attempt
Postmortem — was the regression caught in staging? If not, why not?
anti_patterns: No readiness probe — Kubernetes sends traffic to a pod that has not yet warmed up
Liveness probe identical to readiness probe — restart loop on transient backend failure
PDB `minAvailable: 100%` — blocks all evictions including legitimate node maintenance
HPA scaling on CPU when error rate is the real signal
